description: Lumi Lunar is a solo team: Luana Santos, a Brazilian web developer. Lunar Nav compares lunar south-pole landing sites and dates in seconds: sunlight, line of sight to Earth, NASA Deep Space Network contact, the battery to survive the lunar night, and the uncertainty of every number within ±300 m. Built on NASA/JPL Horizons and LOLA data, validated against NASA PGDA maps, in English, Spanish and Portuguese. I love space exploration and turning complex data into clear tools.
summary:
NASA plans a Moon Base in the lunar south pole region, where the Sun skims the horizon and Earth slips in and out of view behind the terrain. Light and line of sight decide power, survival and communications, and both change with the date and the exact spot. 

Lunar Nav is a web app that answers a planner’s first question for any south-pole site and landing date: when will this site have sunlight, a direct line of sight to Earth and contact through NASA’s Deep Space Network, and how sure are we? It compares sites, shows what a landing delay changes, searches for dates that meet constraints and sizes the battery needed to survive the night. 

It also shows why precision matters: on the Shackleton rim ridge, the published point gets 99.8% sunlight in July 2030, but within 300 m the range is only 48–73%. It adds a 3D view of NASA terrain lit by the real Sun, an AI analyst that answers only from Lunar Nav’s own calculations and cites every number, light and dark themes, and English, Spanish and Portuguese. 

Every number comes from NASA/JPL Horizons and NASA LOLA terrain, carries its provenance and is shown with its uncertainty range. Checked against NASA’s long-term illumination maps (PGDA), it ranks five sites by sunlight in the same order, making NASA data accessible to mission planners, teachers and students.
details:
Your landing just slipped 10 days. Will your site still have sunlight and a line to Earth?

At the lunar south pole, the Sun skims the horizon and Earth rises and sets behind the terrain. A few days or a few hundred metres can decide whether a lander has power and can talk to home. Lunar Nav answers that question in seconds, with open NASA data and honest uncertainty.


Home in dark and light themes: the question every south-pole mission faces, with the Shackleton skyline from NASA LOLA terrain.

Meet Ana (a fictional mission planner). Her landing at IM-2 Athena slipped from 1 to 11 July 2030. Lunar Nav shows her what changed: on the original date the lander would get 0 hours of daylight before its first lunar night; with the delay it gets 250.8 hours. It also shows the battery that night demands: 27.25 kWh for a 363-hour night.


Compare: original vs +10-day landing. Dashed boxes show the spread within 300 m; whiskers show the Sun/Earth disc range.

What it does

  • Explorer: polar map, sunlight %, Earth in view %, contact through NASA’s Deep Space Network, longest dark period, power and battery, and an hour-by-hour timeline.
  • Compare: original vs delayed landing, a search for dates that meet your constraints, and a ±500 m sensitivity map.
  • Sky view: a 360° horizon panorama and 3D NASA LOLA terrain lit from the real Sun direction.
  • Charts: six read-only charts, each with a data table.
  • Analyst: ask in English, Spanish or Portuguese, typed or spoken. The AI (Claude) can only call Lunar Nav’s own calculation tools and cites every number. It never invents data.
  • Report, Methodology and Help: printable PDF report with JSON/CSV/Markdown export, full provenance, validation status, glossary and a guided tour.
  • Light and dark themes, a “Learn” mode with plain-language notes, and three languages.


Explorer: polar map and site readout. Shackleton ridge: 99.8% sunlight at the published point, 48–73% within 300 m.


Hour-by-hour visibility: Sun, Earth, contact, and each Deep Space Network complex (DSS-14 Goldstone, DSS-43 Canberra, DSS-63 Madrid).


A (Shackleton):
Sky view at Shackleton: the Sun stays within about 1.5° of the horizon all month, skimming just above the real NASA LOLA skyline.

B (IM-2):
Sky view at IM-2 Athena: the Sun rises higher but sets behind the terrain, while Earth (blue) dips below the skyline at the end of the period.

A (Shackleton):
3D NASA LOLA terrain at Shackleton on 1 July 2030: the Sun, just 0.9° above the horizon, lights only the ridge crest. Earth is below the horizon.

B (IM-2):
Same moment at IM-2 Athena: the Sun is below the horizon and the terrain is lit only by earthlight. This is why Ana’s original landing date had no daylight.

The finding that changes decisions. On the Shackleton rim ridge, the published point gets 99.8% sunlight in July 2030. But within 300 m, the P10–P90 range drops to 48–73%. Landing precision matters as much as site choice, and Lunar Nav makes that visible.


Sensitivity map: each cell is a point 100 m apart, with its own terrain horizon. Brighter means more sunlight.

How it works and how we checked it
Built on two NASA APIs (JPL Horizons, Scientific Visualization Studio) and four NASA datasets (LOLA, PGDA, DSN 810-005, LROC).

  • Sun and Earth positions: NASA/JPL Horizons (DE441), computed for an observer standing at each site on the lunar surface.
  • Terrain: NASA LOLA elevation models (40 m and 60 m per pixel), with 150 km rays around each site to build the real skyline.
  • Communications: the real positions of NASA’s Deep Space Network antennas in Goldstone, Madrid and Canberra.
  • Validation: compared with NASA’s PGDA long-term illumination maps, the five sites rank in the same order. Known differences are documented, not hidden.
  • Every result shows its source, parameters and an uncertainty range (Sun/Earth disc and ±300 m position), never a single falsely precise number.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Mission planners: a fast, transparent first pass to compare sites and dates, and to see at once what a delay does to power and communications.
  • Teachers and students: a visual, plain-language way to understand why the lunar south pole is so hard, with numbers they can trust and cite.
  • The public: open NASA data made understandable, in three languages.

What is creative about it

  • Uncertainty is part of the answer, not a footnote.
  • 3D terrain lit by the real Sun position at any moment.
  • An AI analyst that is allowed to speak only through verified calculations.
  • A “Learn” mode that adds simple explanations on every screen.


Analyst: every number links to the tool call that produced it (right panel).

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy: hundreds of automated tests (PHP, Python and JavaScript), cross-checks between screens, data audits and validation against NASA references.
  • Accessibility: keyboard navigation, screen-reader labels, light and dark themes and a mobile layout, with 0 automated accessibility violations (axe).
  • Privacy (LGPD, Brazil): no accounts and no tracking; addresses stored only as salted hashes and deleted after 48 hours; a Privacy & Terms page.
  • Honesty: clear limits (no landing-safety assessment) and AI use disclosed on screen and in the repository.
  • Cost control: cached answers and usage limits.


Methodology: premises, known limits and validation status for every number.

Help: who Lunar Nav is for (a mission planner, a science teacher and a university student), with a “Start here” guide, a glossary and a guided tour.

Charts:
Charts: five landing sites side by side (sunlight, Earth in view and DSN contact), with disc ranges and the ±300 m spread. A wide dashed box means the exact landing point matters.

Report:
Report: a printable scenario report (PDF), with JSON, CSV and Markdown export. Every number keeps its source and range.

Privacy & Terms:
Privacy & Terms: what is processed, why, with whom and for how long, plus user rights under Brazil’s LGPD. No accounts, no tracking.

Tools. PHP 8 API, React 18, Vite, Tailwind CSS, three.js, Python (numpy, rasterio, pyproj), JPL Horizons API, NASA LOLA, NASA Scientific Visualization Studio API, Anthropic Claude and ElevenLabs voice. Open source under Apache-2.0: https://github.com/luanasantossnts/lunar-nav

Bonus: Lunar Nav Kids (https://kids.lunarnav.space). The same NASA data turned into three animated missions for children aged 8–12: find the sunniest spot, call home through NASA’s Deep Space Network, and charge a battery for the two-week lunar night. Original mascot, three languages, no AI chat and no data collection.
